property_summary: After calling sudicideAnyone(), the contract's balance remains zero because no funds are sent anywhere.
After calling sudicideAnyone(), the contract's address(this).balance is zero because funds are sent to msg.sender.
After calling sudicideAnyone(), the contract's address(this).balance is zero because all funds are transferred to msg.sender or destroyed.

After calling sudicideAnyone(), the contract has not self-destructed (i.e., its code still exists) because the reference implementation sends funds to msg.sender, while the buggy version self-destructs without sending funds, but the selfdestruct operation destroys the contract regardless of fund destination; however, the observable difference is that the contract's balance is zero after the call in the reference (since funds were sent to msg.sender), whereas in the buggy version the balance is also zero (since no funds were sent), so the key difference is that after the call, the reference leaves the contract alive (codehash != 0) while the buggy version destroys it (codehash == 0).
After calling sudicideAnyone(), the contract's code still exists (codehash != 0) only if the call was made by the owner; otherwise it reverts.
After calling sudicideAnyone(), the contract C should be destroyed (its bytecode length becomes 0).
After calling sudicideAnyone(), the contract's address should have zero bytecode if it proceeded (reference), or still have the original bytecode if it reverted (bug).

After calling sudicideAnyone() as owner, the balance of the contract remains unchanged (reference never sends funds) vs. bug reverts and also never sends funds — but the rule checks that the call does NOT revert when called by owner.
When called by the owner, the function sudicideAnyone must not revert.
After calling sudicideAnyone() as the owner, the contract's runtime bytecode length becomes zero.
